idea.why: A real crew shape rather than one agent doing everything. Collect, sort and present map cleanly onto the brief, and the composer is explicitly forbidden from inventing facts or emitting page chrome, which keeps deterministic presentation out of the model. Loses a little because the dashboard only ever exists as an email body.

structure.why: Purpose-built types throughout, with Aggregate rolling each lane into one item so the agent runs once instead of per message, and the template node holding the shell while the agent supplies only fragments. Two small smells: the Merge exists mainly as a barrier, and executeOnce on the composer is belt-and-braces on top of that.

connections.why: The trigger fans out to the two independent fetches instead of chaining them, each lane runs without cross-talk, and the streams genuinely rejoin before composition. The facts confirm the composer depends on both lanes and nothing downstream starts early; the tail is correctly serial because each step really does need the previous one.

answer.why: End to end it does what was asked and a reader would recognise their request. Two gaps: the recipient is an unfilled placeholder, and delivery is email only, so there is no persistent dashboard URL or history of past briefings.

appraisal: The shape an experienced author would reach for: one schedule fanning out to two independent lanes, an Aggregate on each so the agent sees one batch instead of fifty items, two narrow specialists sharing a single model, and a composer that emits only fragments while the template node owns the document shell. Resilience is thought through, and the sticky notes explain the phases and setup rather than decorating. The weak spot is the join: the Merge is wired as a real rejoin but its combined data is then ignored, making it a pure barrier. The other gap is that the dashboard lives only inside a sent email, with an unfilled recipient and no archived version.
